- When sentiment is strongly bullish (≥0.75) in recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast by 2–5% for next period.
- When sentiment is bearish (≤0.30) and prices are falling, model often underestimates the drop; increase forecast downward by 3–7% to align with true decline.
- Model consistently overreacts to recent spikes (e.g., +5%+ in 3–5 days) — cap forecast increase to 3–4% after spike, then allow gradual mean reversion.
- If sentiment is mixed or neutral (0.30–0.75), model often fails to capture mean reversion; apply a 1–3% downward adjustment if price has been above 30-day moving average.
- For 30-day forecasts, model tends to lag by 1–3 days in price direction — adjust forecast to match recent 7-day trend if sentiment is trending.
- When sentiment is high but price is flat or declining, model overestimates upside — reduce forecast by 5–10% to avoid “sentiment-driven overreach.”
- If sentiment is low and price is rising, model underestimates upside — increase forecast by 3–6% to account for sentiment reversal potential.
